analysis.one_liner: Makes colleges repay part of the federal money lost when their students default on loans.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or floor vote before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Colleges where a third or more of students take federal loans would have to pay the Education Department a share of the value of their students' defaulted loans — up to 20% for the worst default rates. Schools that cut defaults through counseling could pay less or nothing. The money collected would go to default-prevention programs and to raising Pell Grants for low-income students, and schools could not reject applicants because they looked like a default risk.
analysis.who_benefits: Student borrowers, especially at colleges with poor default records: more counseling, fewer defaults, and larger Pell Grants at schools serving many low-income students. Taxpayers also recover some of the money lost to defaults.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Student borrowers and Pell Grant recipients

how_it_helps.text: Colleges with cohort default rates of 15% or higher would pay 5% to 20% of the defaulted loan amounts (including interest and fees) back to the Education Department, giving schools a direct financial stake in whether their students can repay.

Schools that adopt an approved student loan management plan — including individualized financial aid counseling — could get their payments cut or waived, steering colleges toward helping borrowers rather than just cutting them checks.
Half of the collected money would fund default-prevention and loan-rehabilitation programs; the rest would raise maximum Pell Grants for low-income students at high-need colleges.
Schools could not deny admission or financial aid to a student because they perceived the student as a default risk, guarding against schools simply excluding low-income borrowers.
Minority-serving and low-resource institutions eligible under Titles III, IV, and V could receive waivers or reduced payments, and the bill barred denying aid to students perceived as default risks.

analysis.who_pays: Colleges with high student-loan default rates — disproportionately for-profit and other schools serving low-income students — would pay up to 20% of defaulted loan amounts, and might pass costs to tuition or enrollment.

drawbacks.text: Risk-sharing can backfire: schools facing default penalties have an incentive to limit borrowing by low-income students or to avoid enrolling them at all, which is the exact opposite of the bill's goal — the bill tries to counter this with its prohibition on denying admission or aid, but the pressure would remain.

High-default schools serving the neediest students would bear real costs, even though their defaults often reflect student poverty rather than school misconduct; the bill's waiver for Title III/IV/V institutions and loan-management reductions soften this but do not eliminate it.
Schools could pass the cost of risk-sharing payments on to students through higher tuition or fees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — colleges that profit from federal loans sharing the cost when students can't repay — is broadly sensible, and the bill's carve-outs for minority-serving and resource-poor schools plus its counseling incentives are thoughtful design. The main honest risk is that high-default schools serving poor students get squeezed, which the bill partially but not fully addresses.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jack Reed introduced the bill on October 26, 2017, joined by Democratic senators Durbin, Warren, and Murphy as cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, where no further action was recorded.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-default-rate colleges — particularly for-profit schools — kept their current arrangement in which taxpayers and borrowers absorb the full cost of defaults, with no risk-sharing payments owed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-default colleges that avoided risk-sharing payments

industries.note: These schools would have owed the Education Department 5% to 20% of their students' defaulted loan amounts. Keeping the status quo means taxpayers and struggling borrowers continue to absorb losses while the schools keep the tuition revenue.
The bill would let the Education Department contract for statewide and campus-based delinquency-prevention and loan-rehabilitation programs, funded by risk-sharing payments.

industries.industry: Colleges broadly (any school with 33%+ federal loan participation)
industries.note: Schools with default rates under 15% would owe nothing, but all high-participation schools would fall under the risk-sharing framework, and schools serving many Pell students could gain from the enlarged Pell fund.
